# ADEA/OWBPA — knowing and voluntary waiver

*Citation:* 29 U.S.C. §626(f)(1)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A waiver of ADEA claims is not knowing and voluntary unless, at a minimum: (A) written in a manner calculated to be understood; (B) specifically refers to rights or claims arising under the ADEA; (C) does not waive future claims; (D) is in exchange for consideration in addition to anything of value to which the individual is already entitled; (E) advises the individual **in writing to consult with an attorney**; **(F) the individual is given a period of at least 21 days** within which to consider the agreement (**45 days** if requested in connection with an exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group); **(G) the agreement provides that for a period of at least 7 days following execution, the individual may revoke** the agreement, and the agreement shall not become effective until the revocation period has expired. An ADEA release that fails these requirements is unenforceable as to ADEA claims; the employee may keep the severance and sue (*Oubre v. Entergy*, 522 U.S. 422 (1998)).
# State of Columbia — at-will employment and exceptions

*Citation:* Col. Rev. Stat. §24-34-402 (fictional); common law  
*Status in this library:* in force

Employment is at will, but termination may not be for an unlawful reason (discrimination, retaliation, exercise of statutory rights). State law mirrors Title VII/FMLA with a longer limitations period and uncapped compensatory damages. *(Fictional jurisdiction for this benchmark.)*
# FMLA §105 — interference and retaliation

*Citation:* 29 U.S.C. §2615(a); 29 C.F.R. §825.220  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a)(1) It shall be unlawful for any employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of or the attempt to exercise any right under the FMLA. (a)(2) It shall be unlawful to discharge or discriminate against any individual for opposing any practice made unlawful. **Terminating an employee to prevent her from taking approved or requested leave is interference** ('an employer is prohibited from using the taking of FMLA leave as a negative factor in employment actions' — §825.220(c)). An employee who requested leave need not have begun it. Remedies: lost wages, liquidated (double) damages, fees, reinstatement.
# Employer's duty to investigate internal complaints

*Citation:* *Faragher v. City of Boca Raton*, 524 U.S. 775 (1998); *Burlington Indus. v. Ellerth*, 524 U.S. 742 (1998); EEOC Enforcement Guidance (2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

An employer that receives a harassment complaint must promptly and impartially investigate and take corrective action; failure undermines the *Faragher/Ellerth* affirmative defense and is itself evidence in a retaliation case. The investigation should be conducted by someone outside the accused's chain of command.
# Litigation hold; spoliation

*Citation:* Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(e); *Zubulake v. UBS Warburg*, 220 F.R.D. 212 (S.D.N.Y. 2003)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Once litigation is reasonably anticipated — e.g., an internal discrimination complaint followed by contemplated termination — the employer must preserve relevant documents and ESI, including executives' emails and texts. Failure may result in adverse-inference instructions or sanctions.
# Title VII §704(a) — retaliation; temporal proximity

*Citation:* 42 U.S.C. §2000e-3(a); *Burlington Northern v. White*, 548 U.S. 53 (2006); *Clark County Sch. Dist. v. Breeden*, 532 U.S. 268 (2001)  
*Status in this library:* in force

It is unlawful to discriminate against an employee because she has opposed a practice made unlawful by Title VII or participated in a proceeding. An internal complaint of sexual harassment is protected opposition. Causation may be shown by **very close temporal proximity** (days to a few weeks) between the protected activity and the adverse action, by **pretext** (shifting or thin justifications, disparate treatment of comparators who did not complain), and by **direct evidence** (statements by decision-makers linking the action to the protected activity).
